editorials.series: What Counts in the Age of AI?
editorials.title: What Counts as Learning in the Age of AI?
editorials.subtitle: Why higher education must rethink evidence, authorship, and assessment.
editorials.description: An editorial examining how generative AI is changing evidence of learning, authorship, judgement, and assessment in higher education.
editorials.about: This editorial is the first in the ten-part series What Counts in the Age of AI?, which examines how generative AI is reshaping learning, institutional response, authorship, teaching, expertise, assessment, critical thinking, creativity, trust, and what remains distinctively human in higher education.
paragraphs: The other day, I proudly showed my 12-year-old daughter a website I had designed with the help of an AI coding assistant. She adamantly rejected it as my work. Her academic training has taught her that working with AI tools is discouraged, even though she has been using AI effectively to understand complex concepts across the curriculum. At work, I have frequently heard people refer to AI use as if it were something to be concealed rather than acknowledged. Public debates also often frame AI as a competitor to human intelligence rather than as a catalyst for reconsidering how intelligence is demonstrated and assessed.

Every major educational technology has been greeted with predictions of decline. Plato worried that writing itself would weaken memory. The printing press was initially accused of encouraging superficial knowledge and weakening memory and oral scholarship. Calculators were going to destroy arithmetic skills. The rise of internet search prompted concerns about superficial learning, declining memory, and plagiarism. Most recently, the use of AI has raised questions about the authorship, assessment, and legitimacy of work.

However, concerns about innovation have not always been unfounded. Television has contributed to sedentary lifestyles. Social media has also brought well-documented social costs. History shows that every technology creates both gains and losses. The question is how institutions adapt.

We have previously faced similar transitional phases in education. Corpus linguistics and digital databases changed how linguistic research is conducted. Likewise, grammar and language-editing software altered academic writing workflows. Each technology automated something previously considered an essential human skill, yet education did not disappear. Instead, it redefined which skills mattered.

For generations, students and scholars have used tools to handle drudgery. In language, we have moved from dictionaries to spell-checkers and then autocorrect. No serious educator today believes that students must manually memorise every spelling rule to demonstrate mastery of a subject. In mathematics and statistics, we teach students when and why to run a t-test or regression, not how to perform all the arithmetic by hand. EndNote, Zotero, and Mendeley handle much of the mechanical work of formatting bibliographies. The intellectual task is understanding why citation matters, not memorising obscure punctuation rules.
Yet these tools did not eliminate the need for human judgement. They changed where judgement was required. Large language models and generative AI push that boundary further.

We need to distinguish between outsourcing effort and outsourcing judgement. By outsourcing effort, I mean the scaffolding activities that support the real intellectual work but can be offloaded without destroying understanding. Outsourcing judgement, by contrast, involves delegating higher-order processes: evaluation, synthesis, originality, ethical reasoning, taste, and final decision-making. This is where the learner's voice, critical judgement, and accountability reside. Education has comfortably accepted the outsourcing of effort for decades—often centuries—while fiercely guarding judgement.

Previous educational technologies primarily automated procedures or information retrieval. Generative AI automates the production of linguistically coherent reasoning and argumentation. Unlike calculators, word processors, and Google Search, which outsourced execution or retrieval, AI outsources aspects of reasoning expressed through language. Large language models produce explanations, arguments, interpretations, and critiques. This is a qualitative shift, and it helps explain why assessment is under growing pressure to change.

The challenge is therefore not deciding whether outsourcing is acceptable—it already is. The real question is which forms of judgement should remain demonstrably human. Although AI can automate aspects of reasoning and pattern generation, accountability, contextual judgement, and responsibility cannot be delegated.

This means that adaptation must go beyond tool adoption. Teaching and assessment must be redesigned around the kinds of thinking that remain educationally and socially valuable. Traditionally, assessment has often inferred learning from the quality of the finished artefact. Generative AI has weakened the assumption that a polished written product is reliable evidence of individual learning. An AI-generated artefact may resemble expert reasoning, but it is no longer sufficient evidence that learning has taken place.

The mistake is not using AI. The mistake is assuming that assessment designed for a pre-AI world can still measure learning in the same way. Universities have spent the past several years asking whether students should use AI. History suggests a different question: which aspects of intellectual work can responsibly be delegated, and which must remain demonstrably human?
The future of assessment depends not on prohibiting assistance, but on defining the boundary between assistance and judgement.

Returning to my daughter's reaction to the AI-assisted website I built, we can see how education's ambivalent relationship with AI shapes students' understanding of authorship. My daughter readily uses AI to learn, yet instinctively believes that AI-assisted work is less authentically authored. That paradox captures today's educational culture. Every transformative educational technology changes not only how people learn, but also what institutions must accept as credible evidence of learning.

editorials.title: What Counts as a University in the Age of AI?
editorials.subtitle: Why universities cannot adapt to generative AI through isolated policies or tools, and why meaningful change requires rethinking assessment, academic practice, quality systems, and institutional culture.
editorials.description: Universities have moved rapidly from viewing generative AI as an opportunity to treating it as an institutional problem. This editorial examines why meaningful adaptation requires more than new tools or policies: it requires changes to assessment, professional practice, academic identity, quality assurance, and institutional systems.
editorials.about: This editorial examines why universities cannot respond to generative AI through isolated policy changes, software tools, or short-term training alone. It argues that adaptation requires institutions to reconsider assessment, academic practice, quality systems, professional identity, and the organisational conditions through which educational change occurs.
paragraphs: I remember receiving an email at work about Chat GPT a few years ago to gauge the faculty awareness of the tool. The purpose was to formally introduce the tool and enthusiastically encourage its use with careful precautions. Just over 3 years later, I see colleagues frustrated with students’ utter reliance on AI even in simple class tasks. Ironically, the faculty also receive official emails to avoid AI-generated texts for internal faculty competitions. Within a few years, AI had moved from institutional opportunity to institutional problem.

Innovation does not make all efforts insufficient; it exposes limitations in them. The challenge is not merely technological. It is simultaneously logistical, pedagogical, and professional. Imagine spending decades refining an assessment system with thousands of rubrics, hundreds of faculty development hours, lengthy procedures of accreditation, quality assurance and external moderation. AI doesn't just create practical concerns; it also challenges professional identity by questioning long-held assumptions about what it means to teach, assess, and develop expertise. Faculty genuinely worry about fairness, learning, academic integrity and workload.

It is obvious that universities are not merely resisting AI because they fear it. They are protecting decades of investment in assessment systems, quality assurance processes and staff development. They are also confronting challenges to long-established assumptions about what it means to teach, assess and earn a qualification. Should universities redesign the entire system, or first try to fit the new technology into the old framework? Institutions naturally attempt to accommodate disruptive technologies within existing structures before redesigning those structures themselves. However, past investments constrain future choices. Therefore, institutional inertia is rational because universities are behaving like almost every large organisation.

Universities cannot use classrooms as laboratories to experiment with every new idea. They are built for continuity, not rapid disruption. Every untested change has consequences at scale. Historically, institutions first absorb new technologies into existing practices and later they redesign those practices. The issue of AI is different because it challenges the evidence on which assessment relies. Within two years, a technology appears that questions one of its basic assumptions—that a polished written assignment reliably demonstrates individual learning. That is why AI cannot be addressed simply by adding new policies to existing assessment systems.

Universities must encourage innovation while protecting the credibility of learning and qualifications. During technological disruption, those responsibilities pull in opposite directions. Universities are often criticised for moving slowly. But rapid change carries real risks when qualifications affect thousands of students. The challenge is therefore not simply changing faster. The challenge is to change carefully without defending assumptions that technology has already undermined.

The academic community has moved remarkably quickly from enthusiasm about AI to anxiety over its consequences. We need to acknowledge that the greatest obstacle to educational innovation is often not the technology itself. It is the institutional investment in yesterday's assumptions. The challenge is not to make universities change recklessly or defend the status quo indefinitely. It is to identify which institutional safeguards still protect learning and which now merely protect inherited assumptions.

This is the second editorial in an ongoing series on higher education and AI. My next editorial explores a question that has become increasingly difficult to answer: What Counts as Authorship in the Age of AI?

editorials.series: What Counts in the Age of AI?
editorials.title: What Counts as Authorship in the Age of AI?
editorials.subtitle: Responsibility, judgement, and intellectual agency when writing is shared with AI.
editorials.description: An editorial examining how generative AI is reshaping authorship and why intellectual agency, judgement, transparency, and accountability matter more than who produced every sentence.
editorials.about: This editorial examines how generative AI has made a long-standing distinction between writing and authorship more visible. It argues that authorship should be understood through responsibility rather than the mechanical production of text, and introduces the AI-Responsive Authorship Framework (ARAF) as a way of distinguishing intellectual agency, intellectual judgement, and accountability.
paragraphs: Over the past two years, submitting a journal article has quietly acquired another routine step. Alongside declarations of funding, conflicts of interest and ethical approval, many publishers now ask authors to disclose whether generative AI assisted in preparing the manuscript. Academic writing has always been collaborative. Editors refine our prose. Reviewers reshape our arguments. Statisticians strengthen our analyses. Yet we rarely question who the author is. Why does AI suddenly make authorship seem uncertain?

On the contrary, it appears that AI has not broken authorship but merely exposed a misconception that already existed. We have always accepted human assistance, even technological assistance like typewriter, computer, word processor and data analytical software. Generative AI has brought many of these forms of assistance together in a single system, making questions of authorship far more visible.

Yet when AI assists with drafting, authorship suddenly becomes uncertain. That paradox suggests the issue has never been of assistance itself. For centuries, scholarly writing has involved different forms of human and technological support, yet the authorship of the work was rarely questioned. AI has simply shifted the debate from procedure to responsibility. The defining question is no longer who wrote every sentence, but who accepts responsibility for the ideas, evidence, arguments, and conclusions presented. Responsibility—not mere production—has always been the cornerstone of authorship.

An author is not simply the person who typed every word but the person who accepts responsibility for the claims, evidence and conclusions. Authorship is no longer defined by who produced every word. It is defined by who accepts responsibility for the knowledge those words communicate. Publishers now increasingly require statements such as AI cannot be listed as an author because it cannot take responsibility. They have not rejected AI authorship because AI generates text. They have rejected it because authorship carries obligations that extend beyond writing: responding to criticism, correcting errors, declaring conflicts of interest and accepting responsibility for knowledge claims.

To make this distinction clearer, I propose the AI-Responsive Authorship Framework (ARAF), which argues that legitimate authorship in the age of generative AI rests on three interconnected foundations: intellectual agency, intellectual judgement, and accountability. Together, these determine not who produced every sentence, but who can legitimately claim authorship of the work. The first foundation is intellectual agency—who decides what should be investigated? The second foundation is intellectual judgement—who decides what should be believed? The third foundation is accountability—who accepts responsibility? The framework also explains why AI declarations have become a routine part of scholarly publishing. Their purpose is not to admit guilt for using AI, but to preserve transparency by making responsibility visible.

AI has exposed the distinction between writing and authorship that was always there but rarely examined. This makes authorship more important than ever because responsibility becomes the only stable criterion once production is shared between humans and machines.
